summary: Believable aluminium-slat bench on a galvanised cantilever bracket with good end caps and seat number, let down by noisy galvanising, an unexplained block under the front slat and an off-centre single bracket.
critique: Shape: four hollow extruded slats with black end caps on a T-section post with a plate gusset, bolted through a base plate to a chamfered concrete pad. The construction reads correctly and the seat number plate on the front slat is a good touch. Problems: (1) One bracket sits near one end of a roughly 1 m slat run, so about 0.6-0.7 m of slat cantilevers with no support. Real terrace bench runs have a bracket every 1.2-1.5 m, and a tiling module should put its bracket either centred or exactly at the module joint so neighbours meet over it. (2) A solid rectangular block sticks forward under the front slat beside the number plate (close-up view). It reads as an unexplained box, not a clamp or a cleat. (3) The galvanising texture is a high-contrast, uniform blotchy noise, like speckled granite. Hot-dip galvanising is a mid grey (albedo about 0.45-0.55) with soft large-scale spangle, darker zinc oxide toward the base, white-rust bloom in crevices and tide marks near the base plate. (4) The slats are clean and uniform. The top flutes are visible but very faint, there is no anodised sheen variation, scuffing on the front edge, or bird or dirt streaks, and no visible fixings except two countersunk screws per slat. (5) The bracket top plate is a flat slab under all four slats. Real systems use a cast or folded saddle per slat, or a channel with clamp bolts. (6) There is no level change: in a stadium the bracket bolts to a riser or tread nosing. As a standalone prop the concrete pad is fine.
suggestions: Move the bracket to the module centre, or to both ends with half-brackets, so tiled runs have supports every 1.2-1.5 m. Silhouette fix with no extra cost.
Replace the stray block under the front slat with a proper slat clamp: a 40x20 mm U-clip per slat with an M8 bolt head underneath (about 40 tris each), or delete it.

Retexture the galvanising: albedo 0.5 grey, roughness 0.55-0.7, a low-frequency spangle mask (0.5-1 m period) instead of the fine speckle, dark grime gradient over the bottom 100 mm of the post, white-rust (0.75 albedo) in the gusset welds. It can share one 512 trim texture with every other galvanised prop.

Add 2-3 mm fluting to the slat tops in the normal map, a slight brushed anisotropic roughness (0.3-0.4), and edge scuffs and bird-dropping or dirt streaks on the front slat using a vertex-colour mask.
Model a seat-width saddle per slat on the bracket top (4 small bent plates) so the slats visibly sit in something. About 100 tris.
Give the number plate a riveted aluminium bezel and a faint sun fade, and offer a variant mounted on a riser face so it sits on terrace steps directly.
renderer_notes: The grass and flat sky are the test lawn and are not counted.

summary: Correct-scale steel bollard with a domed cap and concrete collar, but the reflective band is oversized and the wear reads as a procedural barcode.
critique: Proportions are about right: roughly 1 m tall and 140 mm diameter, dark grey powder coat, domed cap with a lip, and a concrete collar at the base. Problems: (1) The white band runs from just under the cap to about 30% down, split by a thin dark stripe, so it reads as a white-painted top rather than retroreflective tape. Typical UK bollards carry one or two 50-100 mm bands with a gap of 50 mm or more. (2) The band is matte pure white with no retroreflective look: no micro-prism or bead pattern, no slight sheen, no lifted or torn edges. (3) Mid-height damage is a column of horizontal dashed strokes plus perfectly straight, over-saturated orange vertical streaks. It looks like a barcode, not a vehicle scrape. Real impact damage is a diagonal scuff at bumper height (450-600 mm), with bare grey metal, smeared paint from the other vehicle and rust only where the scuff is old, running down in tapered tear-drop streaks. (4) The collar is a perfectly round slab sitting on top of the ground with one crack line. Bollards are core-set into paving, with a tight mortar ring flush to the surface or a slightly dished fillet, plus dirt and leaf buildup. (5) The shaft has no seam, no makers' mark or sleeve, and no dirt gradient at the bottom. The cap has no anti-vandal fixing or welded seam.
suggestions: Shrink the reflective treatment to two 75 mm bands about 50 mm apart, starting 100 mm below the cap. Use albedo 0.85 with a fine hex micro-prism normal map and roughness 0.35 so it catches light, and add one torn corner. Texture only.

Replace the dashed scuff with one diagonal scrape decal at 450-600 mm: bare metal (albedo 0.55, metallic 1, roughness 0.4) with a smear of foreign paint (white or silver) and short tapered rust runs below it. Rust saturation about 50% of current.

Make the collar flush or slightly proud (10-20 mm) with a soft mortar fillet, add a dirt and grit ring and a darker damp-ground gradient on the bottom 80 mm of the shaft. Optional 6-segment cap weld bead.
Offer 2-3 wear seeds plus a 'new' variant so rows of instanced bollards don't repeat the same scrape.
Keep it at about 200-300 tris. The silhouette is fine and all the gains here are in the material.
renderer_notes: Lawn and sky come from the test scene.

summary: Recognisable as a safe-standing rail seat, but it has no seat back, the top rail is a short stub, and the hinge hardware is crude, so it reads as a simplified kit part.
critique: Shape: a square steel post on a gusseted base plate with a T top rail, a red tip-up seat pan folded up and locked, and a seat number on the post. Problems: (1) Real rail seats (the UK safe-standing type) have a seat back or a back pad integrated with the rail or post, and the folded seat stows in a cradle under the rail. Here there is only a seat pan hanging in front of the post with its underside showing, so it looks like a bare flip seat bolted to a pole. (2) The top rail is a short T stub about 0.8 m wide with flat ends. In use it is a continuous 48-60 mm rail at about 1.0-1.1 m above the tread, running between posts. A per-seat asset should end in a sleeve or coupler so tiles join, or have a flared end cap. (3) The hinge is a bare rod with nuts sticking out past both sides of the pan, with small tabs. Real units have moulded hinge housings or covers and a locking latch. (4) Side view: the seat bracket stack-up (three horizontal arms) looks improvised. (5) The red plastic is a flat salmon pink-red with no UV chalking, no moulding texture, no drain holes in the pan face, and no scuff on the lip. The post is uniformly dark with no galvanised edges or chips.
suggestions: Add the rail-seat back: a 450 mm wide by 250-300 mm moulded back pad in the same plastic, fixed to the post just below the rail, with the folded pan stowed against it under a latch. About 400-600 tris. This is the identity fix.
Make the top rail continuous across the seat width (500 mm pitch) with a joint sleeve at one end so instances tile into an unbroken barrier. Pad the rail with a 60 mm round section.
Replace the bare axle and nuts with two moulded hinge housings (about 60x60x80 mm boxes with bevels) at the pan's back corners plus a small spring-latch block.

Material: plastic albedo about (0.55,0.08,0.07) for a true stadium red, roughness 0.45. Add a horizontal-surface UV fade mask to pink-grey, and 2 drain holes. The post gets edge chips to galvanised grey and a grime gradient at the base.
Simplify the side bracket to one folded steel arm per hinge so the side silhouette reads as engineered.
renderer_notes: Test lawn and sky are not counted.

summary: Right type and scale for an 8 m swan-neck LED street column with a decent lantern head, but the column is a featureless tube on a surface disc with no UK street-furniture detail or weathering.
critique: Silhouette is right: about 8 m tall, a slim column with a swan-neck bracket, and a modern flat LED lantern with heat-sink fins and a photocell node on top, which reads well in the close-up. Problems: (1) The column is a uniform-diameter tube with one spigot joint near the top. UK columns are planted and stepped: a larger root and base section (Ø 140-170) with a flush inspection door about 0.5-1.0 m up, a swaged step to a narrower shaft (Ø 76-89), then the bracket. (2) It stands on a wide round concrete disc on top of the ground. Planted columns go straight into the footway with a small mortar collar. A flange-plate version would show a square base plate with 4 bolts and nut covers. (3) There is no ID plate at the usual height (about 2.5-3 m, black text on white or yellow). Only a tiny yellow mark is visible. (4) The paint or galvanising is a clean uniform light grey with no streaking from the lantern, no dirt splash at the base, and no stickers. (5) The swan-neck bend is very tight and short. Typical brackets use a 0.5-1 m radius with a 1-1.5 m outreach. (6) The lantern glass or optic underside is not visible in any view. It should show an LED array or diffuser with an emissive option.
suggestions: Rebuild the column as root plus base section Ø 160 for the bottom 1.2 m, a door panel inset (300x100 mm, normal-map seam plus 2 lock screws), a 45-degree swage to a Ø 89 shaft, and a spigot to the bracket. About 300 extra tris.
Drop the disc. Sink the root and add a 30 mm mortar collar flush with the ground, or offer a flange variant with a 300 mm square plate and 4 nut caps.
Add an ID plate decal at 2.7 m (number on a yellow or white rectangle) and an optional council sticker. Atlas these with the other street furniture.
Open the bracket radius to about 0.6 m with 1.2 m outreach. Give the lantern underside an LED module grid and an emissive mask for night.
Weathering: dark streaking down from the lantern and bracket, grime gradient on the bottom 300 mm, slight paint fade. Shared trim texture, no extra geometry.
renderer_notes: Close-cut lawn and flat sky are scene, not asset.

summary: Reads as an orange saucer training cone, but it is too tall and steep, the brim is a separate floating ring, and the plastic is a clean toy-like gloss.
critique: (1) Identity and proportions: the reference lists a disc marker as Ø about 300 and 20-30 mm high (a flat disc). This model is a saucer or dome cone about 2.5:1 diameter to height with steep sides. If it is meant as the common saucer cone, real ones are Ø 190-200 mm by 50-70 mm with a shallow 30-35 degree flank and a top hole Ø 40-50 mm. This one is noticeably steeper and taller. (2) The brim is modelled as a flat ring plus a separate rolled lip with a visible gap and seam (close-up), so it looks like a washer sitting under the cone rather than one moulding. (3) The four trapezoid cut-outs are crisp boolean holes with no fillet, and their shape is too large for the flank. (4) Material is uniform saturated orange with a strong specular hotspot, like hard glossy plastic. Real cones are soft, slightly translucent PE/PVC (roughness 0.5-0.6) with a little subsurface glow, grass and mud smears on the brim, scuffs, a moulding sprue mark on top and a faded top surface. (5) No stacking ridges inside or out.
suggestions: Decide the type. For a saucer cone: Ø 195 mm, height 60 mm, flank about 32 degrees, top hole Ø 45 mm with a 3 mm rolled lip. Add a separate flat-disc variant (Ø 200-300, 3-5 mm thick, centre hole) to match the reference entry.
Build the brim and flank as one lathe profile (about 32 segments by 8 profile points, under 600 tris), with the rolled edge as part of the same profile so no gap or second ring appears.
Make cut-outs optional and smaller: 4 slots about 30x15 mm with 2 mm rounded corners, or bake them to an alpha mask on the lathe instead of booleans.

Material: albedo about (0.85,0.32,0.05), roughness 0.55, a slight translucency or wrap-diffuse term if the shader allows, and a vertex-colour dirt mask on the brim plus grass-stain streaks. Provide yellow, red, blue and white colour swaps through a tint parameter.
Add 2 concentric stacking ridges on the flank in the normal map and a small sprue dimple at the top hole.
renderer_notes: The tall shader grass partly hides the brim. That is the lawn, not the asset.

summary: A readable bare-tree silhouette, but the branches are cylinder sticks pushed into each other with blunt or pencil tips, there is no root flare, and the bark is uniform, so it looks procedural rather than dead wood.
critique: (1) Branch construction: in the close-up every child branch is a separate tube that intersects its parent with no collar or blend. Many end in flat cut discs or sharpened pencil points, and several twig segments float slightly or kink sharply. Dead hardwood shows jagged fracture ends, peeled bark, and branch collars swelling at junctions. (2) Twig density is low and too regular: many short twigs stick out near-perpendicular in a uniform pattern. Real dead crowns have tapering fine twig mass at the extremities (or have lost it entirely), with a few long broken stubs. (3) The trunk enters the ground as a straight cylinder in a flat brown mulch disc. Real trunks flare into 3-5 root buttresses over 0.3-0.5 m. The perfectly round mulch ring looks placed. (4) Bark: a pale grey texture with longitudinal stretch streaks, the same on trunk and twigs. Dead trees show patches where bark has fallen off to smooth silver-grey heartwood, lichen (green-grey) on the north side, fungal brackets, and dark wet streaks. The small white things on the trunk read as tags rather than bracket fungus. (5) The scale and lean are fine for a small dead tree of about 6 m.
suggestions: Generate branches as one continuous skinned tube tree: child rings welded into parent rings with a 1.3x collar radius over 0.2 m. This removes the stick-poke look at no extra tri cost (about 3-6k tris for the hero LOD).
End terminal branches with a jagged fracture cap (3-5 offset verts with a pale exposed-wood material) on about 40%, and taper the rest to a point over the last 30% of length. Drop the flat disc caps.
Add a root flare: 4 buttress lobes skinned into the trunk base, rising 0.4 m, and replace the mulch disc with an irregular alpha-blended leaf-litter decal.

Bark material: 2-layer blend of rough furrowed bark (albedo 0.25-0.3) and smooth bleached deadwood (0.55) by a noise mask, plus a lichen tint on the up-facing side. Use triplanar or proper UVs so streaks don't stretch along twigs.
Model 2-3 bracket fungi (flattened half-discs, about 40 tris each, ochre or white with banding) and 1-2 broken limbs lying at the base instead of thin sticks.
Add a cheap twig-card layer (alpha cards, 20-40 quads) at the crown extremities for density at distance.
renderer_notes: Close-cut lawn and sky are scene elements.

summary: Good abandoned-car storytelling (wheels gone, on bricks, POLICE AWARE sticker, cracked windscreen, R-reg plates), but the body is a blocky low-detail hatch with flat opaque glass and evenly spread blotchy rust.
critique: Scale is plausible for a C-segment hatch (about 4.3 m). Problems: (1) The body is slab-sided with hard creases and faceted roof panels. The front is a flat wedge with a slotted grey strip for the grille and bumper. There are no proper headlamp units, no bonnet shut-line set into the wing, and few door shut-lines. The rear hatch has an odd notch in its profile. Mirrors are oversized blobs. (2) Wheel arches are empty dark cavities with a hub stub sitting on bricks. Real stripped cars show brake discs and calipers, the strut and spring, the arch liner, and a rusty underside floor pan and sill line. The body hovering over nothing exposes the missing underside. (3) Glazing is flat opaque navy with no reflection or tint gradient. A broken side window would show the dark interior and shards. The interior is barely represented. (4) Paint and rust: the faded red is a uniform orange-red with rust blotches spread evenly across roof, doors and bonnet, with visible tiling and seams across panel facets. Real neglect makes horizontal surfaces (roof, bonnet, boot) chalky pink and oxidised. Rust concentrates at the arch lips, sills, door bottoms, the windscreen base and boot lip, with bubbling, and there is moss or green algae in panel seams. (5) The bricks are good but read like clean wooden blocks. They need the frog, the mortar remnants and a mix of 2-3 bricks per corner.
suggestions: Rebuild the body from a proper hatch profile (Golf or Focus-like: WB 2.6 m, roof H 1.45 m), add a 1-2 cm bevel on all major creases, and cut shut-lines into a normal map: doors, bonnet, tailgate, fuel flap. Model separate headlamp and tail-lamp units with lens material. About 6-10k tris for the hero LOD.

Fill the arches: a brake disc (24-segment cylinder) plus caliper and a strut tube per corner, a black arch liner, and a simple floor-pan plane with sill and exhaust. Under 1.5k tris and it removes the hovering-shell look.
Glass: albedo near-black, roughness 0.05, a reflection or sky cubemap term, a slight green tint, and dirt streaks at the bottom of each pane. Smash one rear side window to show seats.

Rework the weathering mask by surface normal: up-facing panels oxidise to chalky pink-orange (albedo about (0.6,0.35,0.3), roughness 0.85), vertical panels stay deeper red. Put rust (albedo 0.25,0.12,0.06, roughness 0.9) only at the arch lips, sills, lower doors and seams, with bubble normals and runoff streaks. Fix UV seams so the rust doesn't tile across facets.
Bricks: proper red engineering bricks with a frog, mixed stacks, one tilted, plus some flattened grass or weeds growing at the sills.
Keep the sticker, plates and cracked-glass decals. They are the best part.
renderer_notes: Close-cut lawn and flat sky are scene elements.

summary: One covered main stand with plausible rows, aisles and handrails, plus a low far-side shelter; it reads as a non-league ground but the seating is dark, repetitive and simplified.
critique: The main stand has about 10 rows of dark green and black seats on concrete steps, with vertical aisles, handrails, triangular brick side walls and a front wall. The opposite touchline has a long low covered bench or shelter. Problems: (1) From pitch level the seats read as a dark mass with green rims and little separation. Seat backs need lighter colours or more light to show the profile. Too much lies in roof shadow without bounce light; part of that is the renderer's lack of GI. (2) Every row and seat is identical: no missing seats, no faded or replaced odd-colour seats, no seat numbers, no row letters on the riser ends. (3) The stand has no vomitories, no rear access stairs or concourse opening, and no PA speakers or wheelchair platform. (4) The front wall is a plain green-painted block, and the paddock or standing step in front is absent. (5) The far-side shelter is too uniform and low-detail: a single dark bar on the overall view.
suggestions: Add per-instance seat variation: 3-5% faded (desaturated, lighter) seats, 1% missing or broken, and occasional odd-colour replacement seats. Instance colour attribute only.
Lighten seat albedo to about 0.12-0.18 for dark green, and add a thin lighter rim or roughness break on the top edge of the backs so rows read under the roof.
Paint row letters and block numbers on step risers and the aisle ends, yellow nosings on the aisle steps, and a white handrail-base line. Decals only.
Add 1-2 rear access stairways with a door opening, and a 1.2 m standing paddock or flat concrete strip with a crush barrier in front of the stand wall, which is typical for non-league grounds.
Detail the far-side shelter: visible posts every 3 m, a back wall with club colours and a roof edge fascia.
renderer_notes: No GI makes the under-roof seating darker than it would be. One detail-sheet view (top right) is mis-framed, pointing at sky and lawn, and was ignored.

summary: A believable lightweight steel lean-to roof with a front lattice truss, green columns and a rooflight band; the steelwork reads well, but junctions, gutters and the cladding are simplified.
critique: Good: a green-painted front lattice girder, raking rafters, five slim columns along the front (correct for a cheap non-league stand), profiled sheet roof with a translucent rooflight strip, and correct proportions for the stand depth. Problems: (1) Columns run straight into the girder underside with no cap plates, knee braces or bolted connections, and the column bases have no base plates or plinths. (2) There is no gutter or downpipes at the rear or front eave, no fascia or barge board at the gable ends, and the roof edge is a thin flat slab. (3) The sheeting from above is a flat grey-green with a faint texture: no sheet laps, no fixings, no lichen or dirt streaking down the fall, and the rooflight band is pure white without the yellowed GRP look. (4) The underside shows purlins but the sheeting has no visible profile corrugation in shadow. (5) The roof oversails the triangular side walls with no closure, leaving visible gaps at the ends.
suggestions: Add 300x300 base plates with 4 nuts and a 150 mm concrete plinth to each column, plus 2 knee braces per column into the girder. About 150 tris per column.
Model a box gutter (150x100) along the rear eave with 2-3 downpipes to ground, and a 200 mm fascia or barge flashing on the front and gable edges.

Use a trapezoidal profile normal map (32 mm deep, 200 mm pitch) on both faces of the sheeting. Add a fall-direction dirt and lichen streak mask and tint the rooflights to yellowed GRP (albedo 0.75,0.72,0.6, alpha-ish with lower roughness).
Close the gable ends with a vertical sheet or windbreak panel down to the side wall, which also fixes the light leaks.
renderer_notes: No GI flattens the underside. Shadow-map resolution softens the truss shadow.

summary: The rear and side elevations are plain brown slabs with a cream coping and a single sign panel: correct massing, but no openings or services, so it reads as greybox.
critique: Seen from behind (overall sheet, top-right), the stand's rear wall is a long, uniformly brown-rendered box with a cream concrete coping, a cream plinth band and one dark club-name sign. The triangular end walls are the same flat brown. There are no doors, turnstiles, windows, ventilation louvres, downpipes, lights, CCTV, bins or signage, no brick coursing, no expansion joints and no staining. A real non-league stand back is a brick or blockwork wall with a turnstile block, toilet doors, a tea bar hatch, steel roller shutters, downpipes and plenty of weather staining. The brown has no texture: brick should show coursing at this distance. Nothing around the ground is visible either (no perimeter fence, gate or hardstanding), though that may be site scope.
suggestions: Apply a brick material (stretcher bond, 215x65 mm with 10 mm mortar, albedo variation per brick, at least a 1k tileable) to the brown walls, with a darker engineering-brick plinth course.

Punch openings: 2 steel doors (1.0x2.1 m), a roller-shutter tea bar (2.5x1.2 m), 1-2 high louvre vents and a turnstile pair with a steel mesh cage at one end. Simple insets with a frame trim. About 1-2k tris total.
Add downpipes matching the roof gutter every 6-8 m, bulkhead lights over doors, and the club crest or name board in metal letters on the rear wall.
Weather it: green algae and dark streaks under the coping and downpipe shoes, a damp gradient at the base, and occasional graffiti or fly-poster decals.
Add a perimeter palisade or weld-mesh fence with a gate to frame the exterior at site scale.

summary: Slim columns with 2-4 lamp heads on crossbars and base cabinets are the right type for a step-7 ground, but the heads are tiny and generic and the columns have no structure or detail.
critique: Seven masts of about 15-18 m with small crossbar headframes and a ground cabinet at the base. That is the right idea for a non-league ground. Problems: (1) Lamp heads are tiny featureless boxes with no visor or louvre, no rear driver box, no tilt bracket, no cabling. At club grounds the floods are 0.5-0.7 m asymmetric luminaires with visors, aimed down at the pitch. (2) The columns are uniform thin tubes. Real 15-18 m masts are tapered octagonal sections (root Ø about 300-400, top Ø about 140) with a hinged or raise-lower base, a ladder or climbing rungs, and a flange plate on a concrete foundation. (3) The layout is uneven: three masts on the far touchline, two clustered near one end of the stand side, and one alone. A typical 6- or 8-mast layout is symmetric. (4) The base cabinet is a plain box, with no conduit to the mast.
suggestions: Model the floodlight head as a reusable unit: a 600x450x150 mm housing with a front glass, a visor hood, a rear driver box and a U-bracket tilted 20-25 degrees toward the pitch centre. About 300 tris, instanced 2-4 per frame, with an emissive variant.
Make columns 8-sided and tapered (Ø 350 to Ø 150 over 15-18 m) with a flange base plate, 6 nut caps, and climbing rungs or a ladder with cage on one face for taller variants.
Use a symmetric 6-mast (3 per side) or 4-corner layout for the sunday_league preset, or vary the mirroring deliberately.
Add an access door on the column and a conduit from the base cabinet into the column. Weathering: galvanised streaking.
renderer_notes: Distance views make the heads look smaller than they are. A dedicated close-up would help future judging.

summary: The strongest part: mown stripes, crisp markings, convincing goalmouth and centre-circle wear, and good-looking full-size goals and nets; held back by soft wear blobs, too-even stripes and a pitch that ends abruptly.
critique: Good: alternating mowing stripes, correct markings (penalty areas, arcs, centre circle, halfway line), wear patches in both goalmouths, the centre circle and the assistant referee runs along the touchlines, and full-size white goals with back stanchions and a well-drawn net mesh. Problems: (1) The wear patches are soft, blurry blobs with gaussian edges. Real goalmouth wear is a rectangle in the 6-yard box with ragged, tufty edges, exposed sand-soil, mud ruts and divots, and grass thinning in transition. The penalty-area patch is too large and too uniform in colour. (2) The stripes are perfectly even with identical tone and width across the pitch. Real stripes vary in contrast with viewing angle and have cross-cut stripes on many grounds. (3) Line paint is a crisp pure white of uniform width with no overspray, no fade over worn areas, and lines that stay bright across mud. (4) The playing surface is a flat rectangle that cuts off into the surround lawn with a visible change in tone. It has no run-off, hardstanding path or rail. (5) Nets: the back net hangs cleanly with uniform cords and no sag or drape against the stanchions. No net pegs, weights or tie-backs are visible.
suggestions: Rebuild the wear masks from shaped primitives: the 6-yard box rectangle plus a penalty-spot blot, a goalkeeper's line strip, and centre-spot strips. Use a high-frequency edge breakup (noise at 5-10 cm) and a 3-band material (bare soil 0.35/0.28/0.2 with roughness 0.95, thin grass, healthy grass) with a small displacement or parallax for ruts.
Vary the stripe contrast with view angle (sheen based on mowing direction) and add a 5-10% per-stripe random tone offset. Optional cross-cut pattern preset.
Line paint: modulate opacity with the wear mask so lines fade over bare soil, add 1-2 cm feathered overspray, and use albedo 0.85 rather than pure 1.0.
Add a 1 m pale hardstanding path and a pitch-side rail around the pitch so it doesn't end at a hard edge.
Nets: give the back net 5-10 cm of catenary sag between supports, pegs or ground weights along the bottom, and a little irregularity in cord tension.
renderer_notes: The surround lawn is the test terrain. The visible tile repetition in the distance is the terrain, not the pitch.

summary: Two perspex dugouts with green roofs and bench seats look right for non-league, but the 'tunnel' is a flat bright green box and the dugouts lack seats, fixings and wear.
critique: The dugouts are good proportionally: about 5-6 m long with a clear polycarbonate front and sides, a green roof and fascia, and a bench inside on a concrete pad. Problems: (1) Between them in front of the stand is a flat, saturated green rectangular box that reads as the tunnel or players' entrance. It has no opening, no telescopic tunnel hoops, no door or gate, and looks like a placeholder. Non-league grounds typically have a fenced players' walkway or an extendable tunnel (a fabric over hoops, about 1.5 m wide by 2.2 m high) from a gap in the front wall. (2) Dugout seats are a single flat bench. Typical club dugouts have individual tip-up or bucket seats, sometimes padded. (3) The polycarbonate is a uniform milky white with no edge frame detail, no scratches or water marks, and no reflection. The frames are thin uniform extrusions with no corner joints. (4) There are no technical-area markings (they are present in the overall view, which is good) and no fourth official's board or water bottle crates.
suggestions: Replace the green box with a telescopic tunnel: 4-6 arched hoops (0.6 m apart, 2.2 m tall, 1.6 m wide) skinned with a branded fabric (club green, roughness 0.8) leading from a gate opening in the front wall. About 1.5k tris.
Swap the bench for 6-8 individual moulded bucket seats on a rail inside each dugout (reuse the stand seat mesh).

Polycarbonate material: tint (0.85,0.9,0.92), roughness 0.15 with a smudge and scratch roughness map and slight Fresnel reflection. Add 40 mm aluminium frame profiles at the corners with rivets in the normal map.
Set dressing: water-bottle carrier, kit bag and cones by the dugouts (reuse training props), and the club crest on the dugout fascia.
renderer_notes: Without screen-space reflections the polycarbonate can only fake reflection with a cubemap.

summary: A believable mix of local-sponsor boards (fixed perimeter panels and A-frame boards) with readable typography; too clean and uniform for a Sunday-league ground and with only thin edge detail.
critique: Good: plausible local sponsors (J. Hargreaves & Son, Tidewater, Lumen Sport, Bridge St Garage) with taglines, sharp lettering and varied colourways. Some are A-frame boards leaning back toward the stand, which is typical. There is no screen, which is correct for this level, and the camera gantry tower is a nice touch. Problems: (1) Every board is pristine: no fading, no peeling vinyl edges, no ball marks or mud splash at the bottom, no bent corners, and no tie-wraps on mesh banners. Non-league boards are often PVC banners cable-tied to the perimeter rail, or painted plywood. (2) The boards are flat slabs with a thin edge and no frame, support legs or brackets visible from the front. A-frames should show their back struts. (3) The layout is uniformly spaced, with no gaps, overlaps or variation in height or condition. (4) The graphics use the same type family and layout across sponsors, so it feels templated. Small print is very small and blurry at distance.
suggestions: Add per-board weathering parameters: UV fade (desaturate 10-30%), mud splash on the bottom 150 mm, 1-2 ball-mark scuffs, and peeling corner decals. Driven by the instance seed, no new geometry.
Offer a PVC banner variant: a slightly sagging cloth mesh (2x6 segments) with eyelets and cable ties onto a 48 mm perimeter rail. Cheap and very non-league.
Model A-frame back struts and hinges (2 legs plus a chain, about 100 tris), and for fixed boards add 2-3 posts or brackets and a 20 mm aluminium edge frame.
Vary the type treatment across sponsors (serif, script and condensed faces, a logo mark, phone numbers) and the board heights (0.9-1.2 m).
renderer_notes: The camera gantry tower behind the stand is not judged as part of this category.
